Module 1.title: Fluid Properties, Statics, Manometry and Hydrostatic Forces
Module 1.short_notes:
⚡ High-Yield Exam Summary: Fluid Statics & Properties
  • Newton's Law of Viscosity: $\tau = \mu \frac{du}{dy}$. Dynamic viscosity unit is $Pa\cdot s$ ($N\cdot s/m^2$ or $Poise$, $1 Pa\cdot s = 10 Poise$). Kinematic viscosity $\nu = \mu / \rho$ ($m^2/s$ or $Stoke$, $1 Stoke = 10^{-4} m^2/s$).
  • Hydrostatic Law: $\frac{\partial P}{\partial z} = -\rho g = -\gamma$. Pressure increases linearly with depth in an incompressible fluid: $P = P_0 + \rho g h$.
  • Pascal's Principle: External pressure applied to an enclosed static fluid is transmitted undiminished in all directions. Basis of hydraulic press ($F_1/A_1 = F_2/A_2$).
  • Hydrostatic Force on Submerged Plane: Total force $F = \rho g \bar{h} A$, where $\bar{h}$ is the depth of the centroid. Centre of Pressure ($h_{cp}$): $h_{cp} = \bar{h} + \frac{I_{G} \sin^2 \theta}{A \bar{h}}$. Note: $h_{cp}$ always lies below centroid $\bar{h}$.
  • Buoyancy & Stability: Buoyant force $F_B = \rho_{fluid} g V_{displaced}$. Metacentric height $GM = \frac{I_{min}}{V} - BG$. For stable equilibrium, Metacentre $M$ must lie above Centre of Gravity $G$ ($GM > 0$).
Module 1.detailed_notes:
Module 1 Comprehensive Reference: Fluid Statics

Fluid mechanics governs how liquids and gases behave under external force systems. In static equilibrium, no shear stresses exist ($ au = 0$); only normal compressive stress (static pressure) acts normal to any chosen fluid element face.

Key Formulas & Relations

1. Surface Tension & Capillarity:

$$\Delta P_{droplet} = \frac{2\sigma}{R} = \frac{4\sigma}{D}, \quad \Delta P_{bubble} = \frac{4\sigma}{R} = \frac{8\sigma}{D}, \quad h_{capillary} = \frac{4\sigma \cos \theta}{\rho g D}$$

2. Manometer Equation (Differential U-Tube):

$$P_A + \rho_1 g h_1 - \rho_m g h_m - \rho_2 g h_2 = P_B \implies \Delta P = (\rho_m - \rho) g h$$

3. Curved Submerged Surface:

$$F_H = \rho g \bar{h} A_{proj}, \quad F_V = \text{Weight of fluid supported above curved surface}, \quad F_R = \sqrt{F_H^2 + F_V^2}$$
Module 1.textbook_html:
1.1 Physical Fluid Properties & Continua Hypothesis

A fluid is defined as a substance that deforms continuously when subjected to a shearing stress, regardless of how small that shear stress may be. Under the continuum hypothesis, matter is treated as continuously distributed throughout space, ignoring molecular discontinuities. This assumption holds whenever the Knudsen number $Kn = \lambda / L < 0.01$, where $\lambda$ is the molecular mean free path and $L$ is the characteristic physical dimension of the flow system.

The resistance of a fluid to gradual shear deformation is measured by its dynamic viscosity $\mu$. According to Newton's law of viscosity, the shear stress between fluid layers is directly proportional to the velocity gradient transverse to the flow direction:

$$\tau = \mu \frac{du}{dy}$$

Fluids following this direct linear relation are termed Newtonian (e.g., water, air, light oils, gasoline). Non-Newtonian fluids deviate from linearity according to the Ostwald-de Waele power law: $\tau = K (du/dy)^n$, where $n < 1$ represents shear-thinning (pseudoplastic fluids like polymer melts, blood) and $n > 1$ represents shear-thickening (dilatant fluids like cornstarch suspension).

1.2 Hydrostatic Equation & Manometric Pressure Measurement

Consider an infinitesimal fluid parcel of dimensions $dx \times dy \times dz$ at rest in a gravity field acting in the negative $z$-direction. Force balance between upward pressure, downward pressure, and gravity yields the fundamental Hydrostatic Equation:

$$\frac{dP}{dz} = -\rho g = -\gamma$$

Integrating between free surface depth $z=0$ ($P = P_{atm}$) and depth $h$ yields:

$$P = P_{atm} + \rho g h$$

In manometry, the static pressure difference between two pipeline points $A$ and $B$ containing water (density $\rho_w$) connected via an inverted or upright U-tube containing manometric fluid (mercury, density $\rho_m$) is derived by tracing pressure along the continuous fluid column:

$$P_A + \rho_w g (h_A) - \rho_m g h_m - \rho_w g (h_B) = P_B \implies P_A - P_B = (\rho_m - \rho_w) g h_m$$

1.3 Hydrostatic Forces on Submerged Surfaces & Centre of Pressure

When a flat plate of area $A$ is inclined at angle $\theta$ to the horizontal liquid surface, the total resultant normal force $F_R$ equals the integral of elemental forces $dF = P dA = (\rho g y \sin \theta) dA$:

$$F_R = \rho g \sin \theta \int y dA = \rho g \sin \theta (\bar{y} A) = \rho g \bar{h} A$$

where $\bar{h} = \bar{y} \sin \theta$ is the vertical depth to the geometric centroid $G$ of the plane.

The Centre of Pressure ($y_{cp}$) is the point through which the resultant force acts. Taking moments about the surface axis $O-O$ and invoking the Parallel Axis Theorem ($I_O = I_G + A \bar{y}^2$):

$$F_R \cdot y_{cp} = \int y dF = \rho g \sin \theta \int y^2 dA = \rho g \sin \theta (I_G + A \bar{y}^2)$$ $$y_{cp} = \frac{\rho g \sin \theta (I_G + A \bar{y}^2)}{\rho g \bar{y} A \sin \theta} = \bar{y} + \frac{I_G}{A \bar{y}}$$

Converting into vertical depth coordinates $h = y \sin \theta$:

$$h_{cp} = \bar{h} + \frac{I_G \sin^2 \theta}{A \bar{h}}$$

Because the second moment of area $I_G > 0$ and $A \bar{h} > 0$, the centre of pressure $h_{cp}$ always lies strictly below the centroid for non-horizontal submerged plates.

Worked Numerical Example 3.1 TKMCE University Pattern

Total Force and Centre of Pressure on a Rectangular Sluice Gate

Problem Statement: A rectangular sluice gate $2.0\,\text{m}$ wide and $3.0\,\text{m}$ deep is hinged at its top edge. The gate is placed vertically in a water reservoir such that its upper edge is $2.5\,\text{m}$ below the water free surface. Calculate: (a) Total hydrostatic force acting on the gate, and (b) Position of the centre of pressure relative to the free water surface.

Given Data: Width $b = 2.0\,\text{m}$, Depth $d = 3.0\,\text{m}$, Area $A = 2.0 \times 3.0 = 6.0\,\text{m}^2$. Top depth $h_{top} = 2.5\,\text{m}$. Density of water $\rho = 1000\,\text{kg/m}^3$, $g = 9.81\,\text{m/s}^2$.
  1. Calculate Centroid Depth $\bar{h}$:
    $$\bar{h} = h_{top} + \frac{d}{2} = 2.5 + \frac{3.0}{2} = 4.0\,\text{m}$$
  2. Calculate Total Resultant Force $F_R$:
    $$F_R = \rho g \bar{h} A = 1000 \times 9.81 \times 4.0 \times 6.0 = 235,440\,\text{N} = 235.44\,\text{kN}$$
  3. Calculate Moment of Inertia $I_G$ About Centroidal Axis:
    $$I_G = \frac{b d^3}{12} = \frac{2.0 \times 3.0^3}{12} = \frac{54.0}{12} = 4.5\,\text{m}^4$$
  4. Calculate Centre of Pressure $h_{cp}$:
    $$h_{cp} = \bar{h} + \frac{I_G}{A \bar{h}} = 4.0 + \frac{4.5}{6.0 \times 4.0} = 4.0 + \frac{4.5}{24.0} = 4.0 + 0.1875 = 4.1875\,\text{m}$$
Final Answer: Total Force $F_R = 235.44\,\text{kN}$, Centre of Pressure $h_{cp} = 4.188\,\text{m}$ below water surface.

Part A: High-Yield Short Questions (2 Marks Each)

Q1: Differentiate between dynamic viscosity and kinematic viscosity. Give their SI units.
Ans: Dynamic viscosity $\mu$ measures internal shear resistance under applied shear stress ($\tau = \mu du/dy$, SI unit: $Pa\cdot s$ or $N\cdot s/m^2$). Kinematic viscosity $\nu$ is the ratio of dynamic viscosity to fluid mass density ($\nu = \mu / \rho$, SI unit: $m^2/s$).
Q2: What is the physical significance of metacentric height ($GM$) in floating body stability?
Ans: Metacentric height $GM = BM - BG$ governs the restoring couple acting on a tilted floating body. If $GM > 0$ ($M$ above $G$), the couple restores equilibrium (stable). If $GM < 0$, it overturns the vessel (unstable). Larger $GM$ increases stability but results in uncomfortable, rapid rolling.

Part B: Core Analytical & Derivation Questions (8 Marks Each)

Q3: Derive the expression for the total hydrostatic force and the depth of centre of pressure on an inclined plane surface submerged in liquid.
Marking Scheme Outline: (1) Sketch of inclined plane with coordinate axes, centroid $G$, and centre of pressure $P$ (2 marks); (2) Elemental force integration $dF = \rho g y \sin\theta dA$ yielding $F = \rho g \bar{h} A$ (2 marks); (3) Moment equation about hinge axis $F y_p = \int y dF$ and substitution of $I_O = I_G + A \bar{y}^2$ (3 marks); (4) Final form $h_{cp} = \bar{h} + \frac{I_G \sin^2 \theta}{A \bar{h}}$ (1 mark).

Module 2.title: Fluid Kinematics and Dynamics (Continuity, Euler & Bernoulli Equations)
Module 2.short_notes:
⚡ High-Yield Exam Summary: Kinematics & Bernoulli
  • Flow Descriptions: Streamline (tangent to velocity vector, $dx/u = dy/v = dz/w$), Pathline (trace of single fluid particle over time), Streakline (locus of particles passed through a fixed source).
  • 3D Continuity Equation: $\frac{\partial \rho}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot (\rho \vec{V}) = 0$. For steady incompressible flow: $\frac{\partial u}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial v}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial w}{\partial z} = 0$.
  • Velocity Potential ($\phi$) & Stream Function ($\psi$): $u = -\frac{\partial \phi}{\partial x} = -\frac{\partial \psi}{\partial y}$, $v = -\frac{\partial \phi}{\partial y} = \frac{\partial \psi}{\partial x}$. Streamlines and equipotential lines are mutually orthogonal: $(\frac{dy}{dx})_{\phi} \times (\frac{dy}{dx})_{\psi} = -1$.
  • Euler's Equation Along Streamline: $\frac{dP}{\rho} + V dV + g dz = 0$.
  • Bernoulli's Equation: $\frac{P}{\rho g} + \frac{V^2}{2g} + z = \text{Constant}$. Assumptions: Steady flow, Incompressible, Inviscid (frictionless), Flow along a streamline.
Module 2.detailed_notes:
Module 2 Comprehensive Reference: Fluid Dynamics

Governing Formulations

Acceleration in Eulerian Field: Total acceleration contains local (unsteady) and convective components:

$$\vec{a} = \frac{\partial \vec{V}}{\partial t} + (\vec{V} \cdot \nabla) \vec{V} = \left( \frac{\partial u}{\partial t} + u \frac{\partial u}{\partial x} + v \frac{\partial u}{\partial y} + w \frac{\partial u}{\partial z} \right) \hat{i} + \dots$$

Linear Momentum Equation:

$$\sum \vec{F} = \dot{m}_{out} \vec{V}_{out} - \dot{m}_{in} \vec{V}_{in} = \rho Q (\vec{V}_2 - \vec{V}_1)$$
Module 2.textbook_html:
2.1 Flow Kinematics: Eulerian vs Lagrangian Frame

In fluid mechanics, kinematics describes motion without considering the driving forces. The Lagrangian approach tracks individual fluid particles through time ($ ec{r} = ec{r}(t)$), similar to classical particle dynamics. The Eulerian approach observes fluid properties at fixed geometric field points $(x,y,z)$ as functions of time $t$. The Eulerian velocity vector field is expressed as:

$$\vec{V}(x,y,z,t) = u(x,y,z,t)\hat{i} + v(x,y,z,t)\hat{j} + w(x,y,z,t)\hat{k}$$

2.2 Derivation of Continuity Equation in 3D Cartesian Coordinates

Consider an infinitesimal control volume $dx \times dy \times dz$ fixed in space. According to the principle of conservation of mass:

$$\text{Net mass flow rate into CV} = \text{Rate of mass accumulation inside CV}$$

Net mass flux in the $x$-direction:

$$\text{Mass entering face } x = \rho u dy dz$$ $$\text{Mass leaving face } x+dx = \left[ \rho u + \frac{\partial (\rho u)}{\partial x} dx \right] dy dz$$ $$\text{Net flux}_x = -\frac{\partial (\rho u)}{\partial x} dx dy dz$$

Summing along $x$, $y$, and $z$ axes and equating to the rate of mass storage $\frac{\partial}{\partial t}(\rho dx dy dz)$ gives the 3D differential continuity equation:

$$\frac{\partial \rho}{\partial t} + \frac{\partial (\rho u)}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial (\rho v)}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial (\rho w)}{\partial z} = 0 \implies \frac{\partial \rho}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot (\rho \vec{V}) = 0$$

For an incompressible fluid ($ ho = \text{constant}$), this simplifies to Laplace's equation in terms of velocity divergence:

$$\frac{\partial u}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial v}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial w}{\partial z} = 0 \quad (\nabla \cdot \vec{V} = 0)$$

Caption: Cartesian differential control volume $dx \cdot dy \cdot dz$ displaying mass and momentum flux terms across orthogonal coordinate faces.

Source: Wikimedia Commons / MIT OCW License: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 3.0 Unported

2.3 Euler's Equation and Bernoulli's Energy Conservation

Applying Newton's second law ($dF_s = dm \cdot a_s$) to an inviscid fluid particle moving along a streamline of arc length $s$ inclined at angle $\theta$ to the horizontal:

$$P dA - \left( P + \frac{\partial P}{\partial s} ds \right) dA - \rho g dA ds \cos \theta = \rho dA ds \left( V \frac{\partial V}{\partial s} \right)$$

Dividing by $\rho dA ds$ and noting that $\cos \theta = \frac{dz}{ds}$:

$$\frac{1}{\rho} \frac{dP}{ds} + V \frac{dV}{ds} + g \frac{dz}{ds} = 0 \implies \frac{dP}{\rho} + V dV + g dz = 0$$

This is Euler's equation of motion along a streamline. Integrating for constant density $\rho$:

$$\int \frac{dP}{\rho} + \int V dV + \int g dz = \text{Constant} \implies \frac{P}{\rho} + \frac{V^2}{2} + g z = \text{Constant}$$

Dividing through by the acceleration due to gravity $g$ expresses Bernoulli's equation in terms of heads (units of length, meters of fluid column):

$$\frac{P}{\rho g} + \frac{V^2}{2g} + z = \text{Constant}$$

where $\frac{P}{\rho g}$ is the Pressure Head, $\frac{V^2}{2g}$ is the Velocity (Kinetic) Head, and $z$ is the Potential (Datum) Head.

Module 3.title: Flow Measurement Devices and Viscous Pipe Flow
Module 3.short_notes:
⚡ High-Yield Exam Summary: Flow Measurement & Pipe Losses
  • Venturimeter: Discharge $Q_{act} = C_d \frac{A_1 A_2}{\sqrt{A_1^2 - A_2^2}} \sqrt{2g h}$. $C_d \approx 0.96 - 0.98$ due to low convergence/divergence losses.
  • Orificemeter: $Q_{act} = C_d \frac{A_1 A_0}{\sqrt{A_1^2 - A_0^2}} \sqrt{2g h}$. $C_d \approx 0.60 - 0.65$ due to severe flow separation and vena contracta formation.
  • Darcy-Weisbach Equation: Major head loss $h_f = \frac{4 f L V^2}{2 g D} = \frac{f' L V^2}{2 g D}$. (For laminar: $f' = 64/Re$, $f = 16/Re$).
  • Hagen-Poiseuille Law (Laminar Pipe Flow): Discharge $Q = \frac{\pi \Delta P D^4}{128 \mu L}$. Maximum velocity $u_{max} = 2 \bar{V}$. Shear stress distribution is linear: $\tau = -\frac{r}{2} \frac{\partial P}{\partial x}$.
  • Hydraulic Gradient Line (HGL) vs Total Energy Line (TEL): $\text{TEL} = \frac{P}{\rho g} + \frac{V^2}{2g} + z$. $\text{HGL} = \frac{P}{\rho g} + z$. $\text{TEL} - \text{HGL} = \frac{V^2}{2g}$. TEL always slopes downward in the flow direction unless a pump adds energy.

Minor Losses in Pipe Networks

  • Sudden expansion: $h_L = \frac{(V_1 - V_2)^2}{2g}$
  • Sudden contraction: $h_L = 0.5 \frac{V_2^2}{2g}$
  • Pipe entrance loss: $h_L = 0.5 \frac{V^2}{2g}$, Pipe exit loss: $h_L = \frac{V^2}{2g}$
Module 3.textbook_html:
3.1 Venturimeter: Theory and Discharge Equation

A venturimeter consists of a convergent cone ($20^\circ$ angle), a cylindrical throat, and a gentle divergent diffuser cone ($5^\circ - 7^\circ$ to prevent boundary layer separation and eddy generation). Applying Bernoulli's equation between inlet section 1 and throat section 2:

$$\frac{P_1}{\rho g} + \frac{V_1^2}{2g} + z_1 = \frac{P_2}{\rho g} + \frac{V_2^2}{2g} + z_2$$

For a horizontal pipe ($z_1 = z_2$), the piezometric head difference is $h = \frac{P_1 - P_2}{\rho g} = \frac{V_2^2 - V_1^2}{2g}$. By continuity $A_1 V_1 = A_2 V_2 \implies V_1 = V_2 \frac{A_2}{A_1}$. Substituting:

$$h = \frac{V_2^2}{2g} \left[ 1 - \left( \frac{A_2}{A_1} \right)^2 \right] = \frac{V_2^2}{2g} \left[ \frac{A_1^2 - A_2^2}{A_1^2} \right]$$ $$V_{2,th} = \frac{A_1}{\sqrt{A_1^2 - A_2^2}} \sqrt{2g h}$$

The actual rate of flow $Q_{act}$ incorporates the coefficient of discharge $C_d$ to account for viscous friction losses:

$$Q_{act} = C_d A_2 V_{2,th} = C_d \frac{A_1 A_2}{\sqrt{A_1^2 - A_2^2}} \sqrt{2g h}$$

Module 4.title: Boundary Layer Theory, Drag, Lift and Dimensional Analysis
Module 4.short_notes:
⚡ High-Yield Exam Summary: Boundary Layer & Buckingham Pi
  • Boundary Layer Definition: Region adjacent to solid boundary where velocity increases from zero (no-slip condition) to $99\%$ of freestream velocity ($u = 0.99 U_\infty$).
  • Characteristic Thicknesses:
    • Displacement thickness: $\delta^* = \int_0^\delta \left(1 - \frac{u}{U}\right) dy$ (fluid mass displacement deficit).
    • Momentum thickness: $\theta = \int_0^\delta \frac{u}{U} \left(1 - \frac{u}{U}\right) dy$ (momentum loss).
    • Shape factor: $H = \delta^* / \theta$. ($H \approx 2.6$ for laminar Blasius, $H \approx 1.3 - 1.4$ for turbulent).
  • Flow Separation: Occurs in adverse pressure gradient ($\frac{dP}{dx} > 0$). Criterion: $\left(\frac{\partial u}{\partial y}\right)_{y=0} = 0$.
  • Buckingham's $\pi$-Theorem: If an equation contains $n$ physical variables and $m$ fundamental dimensions ($M, L, T$), the relation can be grouped into $(n - m)$ independent dimensionless $\pi$-terms.
Module 4.detailed_notes:
Module 4 Comprehensive Reference: Boundary Layers

Dimensionless Numbers & Engineering Applications

  • Reynolds Number ($Re = \frac{\rho V L}{\mu}$): Ratio of inertia force to viscous force (viscous flows, pipe flow).
  • Froude Number ($Fr = \frac{V}{\sqrt{g L}}$): Ratio of inertia force to gravity force (open channels, ship wave resistance).
  • Weber Number ($We = \frac{\rho V^2 L}{\sigma}$): Ratio of inertia to surface tension (atomization, droplet formation).
  • Mach Number ($Ma = \frac{V}{c}$): Ratio of flow velocity to acoustic speed (compressible gas dynamics).
Module 4.textbook_html:
4.1 Prandtl's Boundary Layer Concept

In 1904, Ludwig Prandtl revolutionized fluid dynamics by demonstrating that for fluids of small viscosity (like water and air), the flow field around a body can be divided into two distinct zones: (1) A thin boundary layer adjoining the surface where velocity gradients $\partial u / \partial y$ are very large and viscous shear stresses cannot be neglected, and (2) An outer frictionless flow where viscosity effects are negligible and potential flow theory or Bernoulli's equation can be applied directly.

Module 5.title: Hydraulic Turbines (Pelton, Francis, Kaplan) and Centrifugal Pumps
Module 5.short_notes:
⚡ High-Yield Exam Summary: Turbines & Pumps
  • Pelton Turbine: Impulse turbine, High head ($> 250\,\text{m}$), Low discharge. Jet velocity $V_1 = C_v \sqrt{2g H}$. Bucket speed $u = \phi \sqrt{2g H}$ (speed ratio $\phi \approx 0.45$). Hydraulic efficiency $\eta_h = \frac{2(V_1 - u)(1 + k \cos \beta)u}{V_1^2}$. Maximum theoretical efficiency $\eta_{max} = \frac{1 + \cos \beta}{2} \approx 98\%$ when $u = V_1 / 2$.
  • Francis Turbine: Inward radial-flow reaction turbine, Medium head ($60 - 250\,\text{m}$), Medium discharge. Work done per unit weight (Euler's turbine equation): $W = \frac{V_{w1} u_1 \pm V_{w2} u_2}{g}$. For radial discharge at exit, $\beta_2 = 90^\circ \implies V_{w2} = 0$, so $W = \frac{V_{w1} u_1}{g}$.
  • Kaplan Turbine: Axial-flow reaction turbine with adjustable runner blades, Low head ($< 60\,\text{m}$), High discharge. High specific speed ($N_s > 300$).
  • Centrifugal Pump: Manometric head $H_m = \frac{V_{w2} u_2}{g} - \text{Losses} = h_s + h_d + h_{fs} + h_{fd} + \frac{V_d^2}{2g}$. Minimum starting speed $N_{min} = \frac{120 \eta_{man} V_{w2} D_2}{\pi (D_2^2 - D_1^2)}$. Specific speed $N_s = \frac{N \sqrt{Q}}{H_m^{3/4}}$.
  • Cavitation & NPSH: Cavitation occurs when local static pressure falls below vapour pressure ($P < P_v$). Required: $\text{NPSH}_{available} > \text{NPSH}_{required}$.
Module 5.detailed_notes:
Module 5 Comprehensive Reference: Turbomachines

Velocity Triangles & Euler Equation

Euler's turbomachine equation represents conservation of angular momentum across runner blade passages:

$$T = \dot{m} (r_1 V_{w1} - r_2 V_{w2}) \implies P = \dot{m} (u_1 V_{w1} - u_2 V_{w2})$$

Dividing by weight flow rate $W = \dot{m} g$ gives Euler head ($H_e$):

$$H_e = \frac{u_1 V_{w1} - u_2 V_{w2}}{g}$$
Module 5.textbook_html:
5.1 Classification and Principles of Hydraulic Turbines

Hydraulic turbines transform the hydraulic energy of flowing water into mechanical shaft torque. They are categorized based on their working energy conversion mechanism:

  1. Impulse Turbines (Pelton Wheel): All available pressure head is converted entirely into kinetic energy across stationary convergent nozzles prior to entering the runner. The runner operates under atmospheric pressure, utilizing the impulse of high-velocity water jets striking double-hemispherical buckets.
  2. Reaction Turbines (Francis and Kaplan): Only a fraction of the available fluid head converts to kinetic energy before entering the runner; the remaining head remains as pressure energy. Water flows through fully flooded enclosed passages where pressure continuously drops across both fixed guide vanes and rotating runner blades.
